title: Very good (Genesis 1:31)
hook: God made the world freely, out of goodness

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Trinity: one God, a communion of love from all eternity. Your line was love is a communion. Where did you feel real togetherness? Today, that love spills over into a world. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

A Saturday, and a neighbor is building a garden bed nobody asked for. No one is paying her. She doesn't even need the tomatoes; the store sells them. She's doing it because something in her is full and wants to spill over. When the last board is in, she steps back, wipes her hands, looks, and says one word: good. The Bible's first chapter ends with God stepping back and looking, too. Today: creation.
screen: `A GARDEN BED NOBODY ASKED FOR.` → `FULL, AND SPILLING OVER.` → `STEPPING BACK: GOOD.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain. Genesis opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." Then, day after day, as light and sea and plants and animals appear, the same line comes back: God saw that it was good. And at the end, after human beings are made: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." In Hebrew, tov me'od. Not just good. Very good. Second, why God made it. The Catechism says God didn't create because he needed anything. God created freely, out of wisdom and goodness, to share his own goodness. Remember yesterday: Catholics say God was never alone. So, in their telling, creation isn't God filling a gap. It's love spilling over. Third, out of nothing. Catholics believe God created not from some material already lying around, but from nothing at all. In that view, everything exists because God wants it to, right now. Then the question many people carry quietly: can I believe in evolution and still read Genesis as true? The Catechism says the six days are presented symbolically, a picture of God's work, not a stopwatch. In 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth left the development of the human body open to scientific study, while holding that each human soul is created directly by God. In 1996, Pope John Paul the Second said new knowledge had led to recognizing evolution as more than a hypothesis. So a young-earth reading isn't Catholic teaching. Genesis tells who and why; science asks how. Fourth, what very good means for a Tuesday. The Catechism says each creature has its own particular goodness, reflecting something of God. Saint Francis of Assisi sang to Brother Sun and Sister Moon. Pope Francis took his 2015 letter on the environment, Laudato Si', from that song. For Catholics, a world God called very good is worth noticing, thanking, and caring for.
screen: `AND THEY WERE VERY GOOD.` · `NOT NEEDED, BUT SHARED.` · `GENESIS AND EVOLUTION: WHO, AND HOW.` · `EACH CREATURE ITS OWN GOODNESS.` · then, large: `IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one thing in nature. Look for something alive or natural near you: a plant on the sill, a tree through the window, the sky, a dog asleep, even your own breath. Look at it the way Genesis does: made on purpose, wanted into being. Let yourself say, inside: very good. If you pray, you can praise God for it, the way Francis did. If not, simply be glad it exists. The bell holds the time.
Creation. Everything God made freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness: and he called it very good. Today's word.
Your line: it was very good. Today, step outside for one minute, look at one living thing, and say it under your breath: very good. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics profess God as creator of heaven and earth in the Creed at every Sunday Mass, bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis on October 4, and many now keep a Season of Creation each September.

fork.setup: God has finished making the world, including human beings. God steps back and looks. what's the verdict?
fork.reveal: "And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good." only after humans appear does good become very good.

original.note: Hebrew: very good, God's verdict on everything at the end of the sixth day.

trapdoor: what you thought: creation is a story about how long it took.
what it means: God made the world freely, out of nothing, to share his goodness, and called it very good.
what a scholar hears: tov me'od; creatio ex nihilo (2 Maccabees 7:28); CCC 295–301 and 337–339; and Francis's Canticle of the Creatures behind Laudato Si'.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten (opened with the banned "Think of" and told the listener what they felt); "or was lonely, or bored" removed from the Catechism paraphrase (CCC 295 doesn't say it); narrator claims about God ("creation is love spilling over", "everything exists because God wants it to", "worth caring for") now attributed to Catholics.
Douay-Rheims Genesis 1:1 and 1:31 given from memory; confirm.
CCC 295 (created freely, out of wisdom and goodness), 296 (out of nothing), 337 (the six days presented symbolically) and 339 (each creature's own goodness) paraphrased; confirm.
'Only after humans appear does good become very good' (fork reveal): the 'very good' covers all creation at the end of day six; confirm phrasing.
Season of Creation (1 September–4 October) and the blessing of animals on Saint Francis's feast; confirm howItsDone.

Rewritten 2026-10-06 from the five-year map; confirm with the Keeper. 'A young-earth reading isn't Catholic teaching' means it is not required; confirm wording. The six-days myth item was swapped for an evolution item (the six days stay in the teach).
